OpenAI docket as cited; IEA Energy and AI (https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/understanding-the-energy-ai-nexus); NIST AI RMF (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework); EU AI Act Commission texts (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai); BIS export-control notices if cited (https://www.bis.gov); FDA software-as-medical-device guidance if health claims appear; WHO/AT program mate

parts.title: Chapter 9 — AI as Leverage for Ordinary People
parts.excerpt: Objections are on the table. This chapter answers a different question: what can you actually do with the machinery while the window stays open—without…
parts.text: Chapter 9 — AI as Leverage for Ordinary People Objections are on the table. This chapter answers a different question: what can you actually do with the machinery while the window stays open—without pretending every user gets the same lift, and without treating a prompt cheat sheet as a book. Ordinary is not a demographic. It is anyone who runs a life or a small operation without a procurement department: a tenant farmer reconciling invoices after market, a parish volunteer drafting a grant outline, a disabled person routing speech through a captioning stack because phone trees were never built for their body, a two-person shop that cannot hire a second analyst. Institutions buy seats in bulk. Ordinary people buy time in slices and pay the verification tax themselves. The evidence is mixed on purpose. Goldman Sachs and similar banks publish small-business AI surveys through their press rooms—search the primary PDF before you quote a headline about "fully embedded" adoption. Secondary coverage often lands near low double-digit percentages for deep integration while a larger share experiments at the edges. Treat that gap as signal: interest outruns infrastructure. McKinsey's annual State of AI reports are useful for corporate adoption curves and vendor concentration. They are not a census of your neighbor's tool shed. Selection bias toward firms that already answer McKinsey surveys is part of the instrument. Cite them as large-company weather, not as proof your cousin's bakery saved forty hours last month. Government anchors matter when you can match the question to the claim. The U.S. Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy publishes outlook material that occasionally touches automation—read the current-year PDF, not a screenshot. The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook waves sometimes add AI-adoption wording; verify the exact survey item before you paste a percentage into a talk. A number about "using AI" can mean anything from ChatGPT once to a custom model in production. Academic randomized trials tell a sharper story and a humbler one. NBER Working Paper w33795 (Generative AI at Work, 2024—confirm title and authors at publication) reports field-experiment results where contact-center workers gained speed on some tasks while effects elsewhere were uneven. Less time in email is a real outcome. It is not a universal productivity fairy. MIT-linked randomized work on coding assistants (find the current economics.mit.edu draft or published version before citing) often shows gains that split by experience level: juniors move faster on boilerplate; seniors sometimes spend more time reviewing. That pattern is deskilling risk in one direction and skill-boundary management in another—pair junior speed with senior review when the task allows no silent failure. Never blend a bank survey, a corporate consultant chart, and an RCT into one "AI adds X percent" slide. They measure different populations, different tasks, and different definitions of success. Integration is the bottleneck, not curiosity. The honest read of 2025–2026 adoption headlines is a two-tier map. A thin band embeds models into workflows with logging, evals, and fallbacks. A thick band uses hosted chat for one-off drafts and stops there. Neither band is morally superior. They are different depths of design. If you are in the thick band, your next move is not "buy a more expensive model." Pick one recurring task—weekly market recap, parts reorder email, zoning comment letter—and build a repeatable pipeline: input template, model pass, human verification, archive of what shipped. Depth beats novelty. Vendors will keep selling you new interfaces. Your job is to refuse the churn until a measured line moves. Ordinary includes access stacks—and cost bars people out. Assistive pipelines already named in earlier chapters fit every bucket below. They are load-bearing, not demos, and they face the same enclosure risks as any hosted tool: subscription price, privacy policy, feature sunsetting, wrong outputs in high-stakes forms. Affordability is not a footnote. A tool that saves an hour but costs a day of wages is not leverage for the person who needs it. Open-weight models on modest hardware do not solve every access need, but they change the rent equation when they work. Ordinary must include people whose "work" is participating in public life when the default interfaces were hostile. Six buckets—not six magic spells. Appendix B will expand this list. The chapter keeps one worked example per bucket plus the verification step that separates leverage from lottery. Learn. You are studying a new irrigation scheduling method and the extension PDF is eighty pages. You use a model to generate questions and a one-page glossary of terms you do not know—not to replace the PDF. Verification: open the primary bulletin and check every definition the model gave you. If a term is wrong, the failure mode is obvious before you bet a standpipe on it. Plan. You need a crop rotation sketch for a three-field lease with a cover-crop goal and an equipment constraint. You ask for three scenarios with explicit assumptions (days to maturity, equipment passes, frost window). Verification: run the scenarios past your soil test, your lease clauses, and—if you have one—your extension agent. The model does not know your neighbor's hog lagoon. Draft. A food hub needs a plain-language email to members about a pickup time change. The model produces a draft in the hub's tone if you feed two prior emails. Verification: a human reads for wrong dates, wrong fees, and accidental promises. Low stakes, still worth a calendar check. Code. A maintainer adds a script to parse CSV exports from a co-op ledger. The model proposes boilerplate; you run tests, read diffs, and keep the parts you can debug at 11 p.m. Verification: the test suite and one manual edge case you invent (empty file, duplicated row). Mixed-experience teams should pair junior speed with senior review—the RCT pattern above. Admin. Invoices, grant deadlines, license renewals—the paperwork that eats evenings. The model sorts a pile into buckets with dates and drafts reminder language. Verification: cross-check every date against the PDF in the envelope pile. Models confuse fiscal years easily. Research. You need to know whether a state bill still affects small slaughter facilities. The model summarizes with citations you can click. Verification: read the statute section headings yourself or pay someone licensed. Research buckets fail loudest when users skip the click. Across buckets the design pattern is the same: model proposes, human disposes, archive proves what shipped. What this chapter refuses to sell. If you cannot tie a ROI claim to a labeled survey, a cited paper, or your own logged before/after on one task, do not put it on a slide. Prompt tricks age in weeks; design lasts a season—this is not a cheat sheet chapter. Vendor demos are cherry orchards; ask for task-specific error rates on work like yours or run your own eval. And no replacement pitch for skilled humans in high-trust roles—medicine, law, structural engineering, food safety sign-off. The same Monday can include a grazing log on paper, a spreadsheet, and a local model rewriting column headers so the export matches what your co-op's portal expects. Neither identity wins. The task wins when the verification step matches the harm if the output is wrong. A systems-first reader might ship a small RAG stack over municipal PDFs so neighbors can query zoning without reading three hundred pages. A place-first reader might use speech-to-text to draft testimony for a water board hearing after a long field day. The leverage is not the brand on the model. It is calendar returned with errors caught before they become someone else's emergency. Pick one bucket. Pick one recurring task inside it. Log one week: minutes before, minutes after, one error caught in verification, one error that would have shipped

parts.title: Chapter 10 — Why This Era Is Temporary
parts.excerpt: You have seen what ordinary people can build while access stays cheap enough to test. This chapter asks the harder follow-up: what closes the window—and…
parts.text: Chapter 10 — Why This Era Is Temporary You have seen what ordinary people can build while access stays cheap enough to test. This chapter asks the harder follow-up: what closes the window—and why temporary is not prophecy. Temporary is not a countdown to doom. It is a description of pressure: law that adds compliance cost, export rules that choke compute supply, pricing that moves faster than your budget, terms of service that rewrite what you may do with a model you thought you owned, and concentration that makes one vendor's outage your week's emergency. The era of hosted frontier inference and periodic open-weight releases feels open because you are living inside it. That feeling is accurate. It is not a guarantee. The EU AI Act is a calendar, not a mood. European product-safety law for AI now has dates you can mark on a wall calendar—verify every date against the European Commission's regulatory framework page and the AI Act Service Desk timeline before you print, because Digital Omnibus negotiations and simplification packages can shift high-risk timing without changing the core point: obligations arrive on a schedule. As of the Commission's published implementation timeline (re-read at publication): prohibited practices and AI literacy provisions under the general framework took effect 2 February 2025; governance for general-purpose AI models, national authority structures, penalty frameworks, and EU-level bodies begin to bite for GPAI providers on 2 August 2025; the bulk of remaining rules, including transparency obligations under Article 50 and many Annex III high-risk categories on the non-embedded path, land on 2 August 2026; high-risk AI embedded inside regulated products tied to Annex II sectors follows on 2 August 2027. The regulation text lives on EUR-Lex (CELEX:32024R1689). Read the primary text when you need a precise category definition—not a thread that conflates "chatbot" with "safety component in a medical device." What this means for an ordinary builder is not "Brussels banned thinking." Most systems the Commission describes publicly sit in minimal-risk buckets. The honest read is procurement friction: a clinic, school, co-op, or municipal office that waited for a trusted compliance path may finally adopt tools they avoided when the liability was vague. A solo operator shipping a fine-tuned model into the EU without reading Annex III may discover they are building documentation they did not budget for. Both outcomes can be true in the same year. Bruegel's analysis of the Act as "premature or precocious" regulation is worth pairing with the Commission overview—not as a verdict, but as a reminder that implementation risk is its own variable. Rules on paper and rules in a working procurement department are different objects. US export controls treat advanced compute as a choke point. The Bureau of Industry and Security publishes advanced computing and semiconductor rules through Federal Register notices and agency guidance PDFs. If you cite export posture, cite BIS primary materials for the date you print—not a podcast summary of "what China can't buy." The steelman is not cynical cover for monopoly. Advanced compute controls are defended as slowing diversion of chips and model weights into military, surveillance, and proliferation-relevant stacks. Paired domestic fab policy—CHIPS-class investment narratives—often frames the same decade as "paying for resilience" rather than only starving rivals. Think-tank analysis such as CSIS work on updated export controls belongs in your notes alongside the agency rule, labeled as interpretation. For a builder outside the Fortune 500, the practical effect is supply-side: fewer GPUs in the secondary market at prices you could stomach, longer lead times on clusters, licensing uncertainty for weights hosted across borders, and a research landscape where where the model runs becomes a legal question—not only a latency question. That is pressure on the window. It is not proof the window is already shut for everyone everywhere. It is proof the window has politics welded to the hinges. Cloud concentration is an enclosure you can measure. Most ordinary leverage runs on rented metal whose price, terms, and feature set change on someone else's roadmap. Cloud pricing pages have histories. If you claim inference "used to be cheaper," archive.org snapshots of provider pricing tables are your friend—not a screenshot from a forum. API deprecation posts on OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and smaller hosts are existence proof that the model ID in your script is a lease, not a deed. Sunsets can track abuse prevention, copyright pressure, safety retrofits, or endpoints that no longer pay for themselves. One documented changelog read in good faith is enough to steelman a vendor before you imply bad faith across the board. The counter-steelman matters: concentrated clouds sell patch velocity, physical security, compliance attestations, and global routing many small organizations cannot home-build at the same standard. Plenty of SMEs choose rent because self-hosting would be less safe—not only because they love oligopoly. That is true. It does not follow that rent is forever at today's price, or that today's acceptable terms survive the next funding round. Terms of service are the quiet enclosure. Training opt-out defaults, logging policies, enterprise-only features, geographic restrictions, and "acceptable use" clauses that expand without a vote—these rewrite what "your stack" means while your integration deepens. Your one-week task log assumes you can rerun the pipeline next month. ToS assumes you read what changed at 2 a.m. Connectivity and compute are not the same bottleneck. ITU Facts and Figures reporting (verify the current edition at publication) is the sober anchor for global inequality claims: billions still offline or under-connected, regional and income gaps that no product launch erases. Use one careful paragraph here—not a deterministic "West locks the Global South out of AI forever" stack. Mobile-first leapfrogging and regional investment complicate single-story rhetoric. The narrow claim that holds: a person with intermittent connectivity and no local GPU faces a different window than a researcher with a cluster allocation—and both may be "using AI" in a survey item that means nothing comparable. Connectivity pressure and compute pressure stack; they are not interchangeable. If your exit ramp assumes hardware you can buy retail, name who that assumption excludes—and whether open-weight releases on modest machines change the rent equation for them, partially, sometimes, with work. Steelman the goods before you steelman the squeeze. This chapter fails if it reads like a conspiracy wall. The mechanisms above are defensible tensions: product safety, diversion control, reliability at scale, abuse prevention, proportionality fights in live legislation. Regulation can give institutions a procurement path they trust—schools, clinics, utilities—so assistive and operational tools ship with documentation instead of shadow IT. Export controls express a real preference: fewer surprise wars driven by mass surveillance and autonomous weapons pipelines; the dispute is cost-sharing and collateral damage to researchers, not whether any line exists. Cloud rent buys uptime ordinary teams cannot replicate in a closet rack without learning hard lessons about cooling, patching, and breach response. Model sunsets sometimes retire endpoints that were being abused at scale or that courts and licensors made uneconomic—not only to extract more rent from captive integrations. Digital Omnibus and simplification lobbying are the Commission's counter to "Brussels crushed SMEs"—rules may stretch because lawmakers heard proportionality complaints. Re-pull the Service Desk FAQ when you draft; live negotiation beats frozen outrage. Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to design as if both halves are true: the window is useful becau

parts.text: Chapter 11 — Use the Window Without Becoming Owned Law, export rules, pricing, terms of service, and concentration narrow access from the outside. This chapter names what happens inside your week while those clocks tick—attention, habit, account security, and the difference between a tool you deploy and a feed that deploys you. Owned is not a mood. It is a structure: defaults you never chose, sessions that outlive the task, credentials scattered across vendors, skills that thin because the interface always offers the next completion, and a body trained to check before the body trained to finish the work. The window stays useful only if you can walk through it and still recognize your hands on the other side. Loops are designed. Average effects are small. Both can be true. Screen-time panic already ran its course in public debate. The peer literature matters here for a different reason—not to declare phones harmless, but to separate mechanism from headline. Orben and Przybylski's time-use-diary work in Psychological Science (2019; verify effect sizes and wording at publication) finds associations between digital technology use and adolescent psychological well-being that are small relative to many other life variables in the same datasets. Large samples. Careful measurement. A result that should humble anyone writing a sermon about "destroyed generations." That is true. It does not follow that retention design is imaginary. A social feed and a field notebook can both glow on glass. They do not share a business model. One sells return visits priced in attention and data; the other sells nothing while you write unless you later attach a subscription. The small average effect in population studies does not erase the engineering fact that infinite scroll, variable reward schedules, and notification stacks exist because they increase time-on-platform. It means moral panic is a blunt instrument—and blunt instruments get wielded at the wrong target while the design keeps shipping. WHO screen-time guidance for children (re-pull the current age brackets at publication) is worth citing when you touch parenting: the organization distinguishes sedentary screen time from physical activity and sleep displacement—not "screens evil, period." Use clinical addiction language sparingly. Pathologizing an ordinary reader's Tuesday night check-in is not care. Describing a product built to maximize sessions is not denial. Your design question is sharper than "how many hours": who owns the interrupt? If the tool can ping you but you cannot silence it without fighting settings buried three menus deep, the ownership line has already moved. Digital minimalism is a foil, not an enemy. Cal Newport's Digital Minimalism and related "deep work" writing gave millions of people permission to say no to default stacks. The steelman: modern knowledge work fragments by design; protecting blocks of uninterrupted attention is a legitimate craft move, not Luddism. A welder does not take calls inside the spark zone. A grazier on fence repair does not owe the group chat a minute-by-minute photo stream. A municipal engineer reviewing a heat-recovery sketch needs the same protected hour—even if the "distraction" is another tab, not a phone buzz. The strawman to refuse: minimalism as identity purity—the person who brags about no smartphone while outsourcing every coordination friction to someone else's device and labor. Or minimalism as one-size austerity that treats assistive tech as optional luxury. Reducing noise is not the same as reducing capability. Minimalism fails as a universal prescription when it treats all digital contact as fungible. Your co-op's shared spreadsheet is not your cousin's outrage loop. A local model on a laptop is not a casino feed. The filter is not "less screen." The filter is whether this object serves the target you named—autonomy, land, resilience, paid work—or rents your nervous system to someone else's metric. Practical middle: protocols, not vibes. A weekly "office hours" window for messages. A phone drawer during one physical task. A browser profile that cannot open social sites during drafting. A grazing log on paper first, photo second—because the thumb wants to edit before the eye has counted. None of that requires pretending the peer literature says catastrophe. It requires admitting you are fighting product managers, not weak will. Skills maintenance is maintenance, not nostalgia. Ericsson-style deliberate practice is easy to misquote into "ten thousand hours" folklore. Light touch only: skills decay when feedback loops shorten. If the tool always drafts, you stop drafting; if the map always routes, you stop reading terrain; if the model always summarizes the ordinance PDF, you stop noticing which clause actually binds the setback. Trade craft makes the point without romance. An apprentice electrician still turns screws under supervision after the power-tool arrives. The tool speeds the hand; it does not replace the code book in the pocket. AI-assisted desk work fails the same way when "good enough" output ships without a human who can spot a wrong unit, a wrong species in a planting plan, or a wrong assumption about who holds the easement. Place-first example: you use a model to draft soil-amendment rates from lab PDFs. The verification step is a spreadsheet you still understand—formulas visible, units checked against the lab's original table, one row spot-calculated by hand. Systems-first example: you use codegen to scaffold an API client. The verification step is one request replayed in curl with headers you typed, not only a green test badge. Same rule: the window should not close over a skill you no longer possess when the vendor changes the UI. Security hygiene is sovereignty infrastructure. CISA's public guidance is boring on purpose—verify current URLs at publication. Password managers. Phishing recognition. Multi-factor authentication on email and cloud accounts that gate your manuscript, your co-op books, your domain registrar. Patched operating systems on the machine that holds keys. Backups you have restored once, not backups you intend to restore. This is not paranoia. Terms of service are quiet enclosure; account takeover is the loud version: you lose the repo, the newsletter list, the grant login, the irrigation controller dashboard because one reused password sat in a breach dump from a forum you forgot you joined. Steelman the vendor: hosted platforms ship patch cadence and physical security many small shops cannot replicate in a closet rack. True. It does not follow that your identity perimeter should be thin. Hygiene shifts the asymmetry slightly back toward you without pretending you can out-engineer a nation-state. A concrete stack sketch, with tradeoffs disclosed—not a product ad. Identity layer: password manager plus MFA on mail, DNS, bank, and cloud—costs an afternoon of setup and recovery codes stored offline. Work layer: offline-capable notes with periodic export—sync conflicts you resolve yourself. Inference layer: local model for drafts plus hosted model for tasks that need scale—two eval habits, two privacy postures. Comms layer: one channel for urgent, one for async—colleagues must learn your map. Diversifying tools is not hoarding. It is avoiding single-vendor capture of your attention, your files, and your inference path—enclosure experienced at human scale. Local-first is a posture, not a purity badge. The local-first software movement pushes data toward devices you control, with collaboration layered on top—cite specific tools you actually run and disclose sync and backup behavior at publication. The steelman: latency, privacy, and survivorship when the uplink dies mid-harvest week. The honest counter: conflict resolution, backup discipline, and the social cost of asking neighbors to install another app. You do not owe the movement a religion. You owe yourself a test: if this service vanished tomorrow, what do you still

parts.text: Chapter 12 — Build Your Exit Ramp You were asked to keep your attention, your credentials, and at least one offline copy of work that matters while the hosted stack still answers. This chapter asks what you are building toward when the window narrows: land you can work, savings that survive a bad quarter, a legal shape for paid work, or a local enterprise that does not depend on a single platform's mood. An exit ramp is not a mood board. It is material infrastructure—paperwork, cash buffers, skills that transfer, relationships with institutions that outlast one vendor contract. The machines from prior chapters keep running whether you leave or stay. The question is whether you have a path that does not require their permission forever. Five buckets, one chapter—not five fantasies. This book has already mixed place-first and systems-first examples. The same split applies here. You may be a land seeker trying to translate savings into tenure. You may be a worker stitching wage work to self-employment without pretending the transition is frictionless. You may be a creator trading audience for income—with odds that deserve honesty, not coaching-industry math. You may be a family household balancing care, health, and cash flow across more than one earner. You may be a local builder opening or keeping a small enterprise on a Main Street that did not ask your opinion about data-center power rates. Most readers occupy more than one bucket at once. A grazier with a side contract and a Substack is not a category error. A municipal engineer saving for a homestead while consulting on heat recovery is not cheating the argument. The buckets are planning lenses, not identities to perform online. What this chapter will not do: sell you a guru timeline, quote MLM "average income" slides, or treat YouTube follower counts as a retirement plan. What it will do: name credible ranges, point to primary sources you can re-pull for your county and year, and front-load the places where you need a CPA, attorney, engineer, or extension agent in the room—not a paragraph in a book. Land seekers: the ladder is real; your county is the rung. USDA land values are a structural fact, not a motivational poster. Here the same numbers do a different job: translation into savings targets and timeline honesty. The National Agricultural Statistics Service publishes annual land-value and cash-rent summaries with state and regional spreads. NASS cropland averages in recent releases sit in the low thousands per acre nationally—with state lines that swing by an order of magnitude. That spread is the point. A national average tells you the direction of the ladder. It does not buy you a field in the county where you actually want to stand. Use NASS and ERS the way a builder uses a tape measure: update before you cut. Cash rent per acre matters as much as purchase price when you are modeling entry on leased ground. Beginning-farmer publications from USDA's Economic Research Service—land access hubs, credit and tenure summaries—return to the same stubborn facts: entry is expensive, transitions are slow, credit is uneven, and who holds title shapes who can experiment. ERS is not a mortgage broker. It is a sober counterweight to forum posts that treat "five acres" as a universal unit. Savings math belongs in ranges, not precision theater. If cropland in your target county clusters around a band you verify from NASS—and you are aiming for a down payment, closing costs, equipment reserve, and one year of operating buffer—work backward from your band, not from a meme about "ten acres." Add lease-option clauses, seller financing, cooperative purchase models, and USDA program pages only as pointers: FSA loan categories, conservation easements that change what "ownership" means, land-link programs that match retiring operators with entrants. Each path runs through different paperwork and risk. None of them removes the need for local professionals. Tenure repeats because sticker price hypnotizes people. A cheap listing with a short lease and no improvement clause is not an exit ramp. It is a depreciation sink—the same mistake as signing a cloud contract you cannot export from because the monthly fee felt manageable on day one. If your ramp includes land, write down whether you mean ownership, long-term lease, cooperative access, or something else—and what happens if the landlord sells, dies, or raises rent the year you finally fixed the drainage. Place-first example: you model three entry paths for the same county—lease with option, cooperative share purchase, and straight fee simple—each with a cash timeline you update quarterly from NASS and your own bank statement. Systems-first example: you model the same discipline for a small shop: equipment reserve, three months of operating expenses, and a legal entity that separates personal liability from contract work. Different surfaces. Same rule: ranges verified from primaries, not vibes from a thread. Zoning, water rights, easements, and entity choice belong in rooms with people licensed for your jurisdiction—not in this paragraph. Workers and formation: statistics without folklore. Many households already combine wage work, seasonal labor, contract gigs, and speculative bets on flexibility. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey self-employment categories move year to year—check the current table at citation time rather than freezing a percentage into a meme. The broader truth is stable: formation is a process, not a Friday-afternoon PDF. Registering an LLC does not replace a client pipeline. Getting an EIN does not replace bookkeeping. Leaving a W-2 job without health coverage mapped for your household is not autonomy. It is a different constraint you may or may not have priced. If you cite Occupational Outlook Handbook wage tables for a path you are considering—electrician, nurse, software developer, farm manager—use them as labor-market weather, not as a promise about your résumé in your metro. Median wage is not your offer letter. Growth projections are not a schedule. The Census Bureau publishes nonemployer statistics—businesses with no paid employees, often sole proprietors and side operations. Useful for scale: a large count of tiny entities does not mean a large count of people who replaced a salary. Many nonemployer lines are intermittent, hobby-adjacent, or loss-leaders for something else. Treat "side business" counts as evidence of experimentation, not evidence that experimentation succeeds. Name the first dollar of revenue you need and by what date, separate from the story you tell friends. Separate accounts early enough that tax season is not archaeology. Decide whether your ramp requires benefits through a spouse's plan, a marketplace policy, or a trade-off you document in writing. Keep one skill that converts to wage income if the bet slips—a license, a certification, a trade union card, a stack you can deploy as a contractor. Systems-first reader: your ramp might be consulting revenue that funds a local inference lab and a larger emergency fund before you reduce W-2 hours. Place-first reader: your ramp might be market gardening that funds equipment while you keep winter wage work—seasonality in the model, not surprise in February. Mixed reader: you already know which months cash in and which months only cash out. Put that curve on one page before you argue about tools. Creators and audience: Pew with the methodology page open. Platform work is real work. It is also a lottery with transparent odds if you read the surveys instead of the highlight reels. Pew Research Center publishes creator-economy and platform studies with explicit methodology sections—sample frames, weighting, question wording. Before any percentage lands in your plan, read the methods PDF for that release. Pew's 2024 work on news influencers and YouTube, and followership studies on platforms such as TikTok, are useful for a narrow claim: attention concentrate

parts.text: Conclusion — Build the Better Alternative You ended the prior chapter on objects you can still touch when the terms change: savings that compound, a lease you have read, a client who pays you directly, a field notebook that never required a login. This chapter names what those objects add up to. Not a brand. Not a manifesto. A design problem you have already been solving in pieces—sometimes with soil under your nails, sometimes with a diff open at midnight, often with both in the same week. Build the better alternative is not a call to win a debate. It is a call to ship arrangements that survive a bad Tuesday. The argument through twelve chapters was never that tools are innocent. Tools are neutral in the textbook sense and guilty in the incentive sense. Society blames the hammer because blaming design requires admitting who drew the blueprint. Data centers and dairy coolers share load shapes; grazing plans and inference stacks share the same transitional stain when you move a ledger line before the story is clean enough to post. AI arrived as mechanism, objection, ordinary use, temporary enclosure, and attention rent—then as an exit ramp you could walk without pretending the ladder was free. What repeats is not a gadget. It is design literacy: name the target, trace who benefits from delay, verify before the error becomes someone else's emergency, keep an offline path for work that should survive a terms-of-service email. The narrowing window from the introduction was the overlap of clocks—release cadence, lease renewal, land price, export rule—while capable tools still sat on ordinary tables. That window is closing in the sense that defaults harden. It remains open in the sense that builders still move variables on ground they do not own yet and hardware they did not buy new. Two builders from earlier pages are enough to show what "alternative" means in practice. They are not saints. They are people who refused to let the ideal delay become the incumbent's free pass. The grazier on rented ground did not wait for a certification badge that would impress a comment thread. The lease allowed moves; the extension agent had local data; the soil test moved on a schedule the literature could defend for that place—not for every biome on earth. Multi-paddock grazing under those constraints is transitional betterment: a measured line on organic matter and stocking pressure while the landowner still holds title and the carbon-offset salesman still sends brochures built on claims the book already steelmanned and corrected. The alternative is not "cattle save the climate." It is stocking as protocol you can explain to your kids without lying. The food hub coordinator did not confuse a model with membership. A pickup time changes; two prior emails set tone; the model drafts plain language; a human reads for wrong dates, wrong fees, and accidental promises. Low stakes—still worth a calendar check. The alternative is not "AI runs the co-op." It is calendar returned with errors caught before they become forty families at the wrong dock. The same design pattern runs in a maintainer's CSV script, a zoning RAG stack over municipal PDFs, speech-to-text after a long field day: model proposes, human disposes, archive proves what shipped. Between those examples sits the systems-side existence proof from the same transitional chapter: inference on hardware you already own, licenses read as design documents, a pipeline that can exist without every token crossing a dashboard tuned for engagement. None of that promises purity. It proves the architecture is choosable while the defaults still allow the choice. Micro-hydro on a village co-op, solar dryers maintained by trained technicians, district heat coupled to a second user with a contract long enough to justify pipe—the book's earlier chapters named the same move at different scales. Appropriate for whom. Right-sized for the load. Paperwork before brand. An alternative is not a utopia you announce. It is a stack you can inspect. At the bottom: the build sentence you were willing to embarrass yourself with—what you are building and why. Above that: structural facts you update instead of folklore—land bands, lease clauses, cash months, export rules, the dependency you could lose in thirty days. Above that: tools chosen by task harm, not by moral perfume or vendor hype. At the top: objects and relationships that do not reset when a price doubles—a savings line, a direct client, a co-op book, a grazing log on paper before the photo, an email list that is not a platform graph. Purity says wait until the story is clean. Cynicism says the fix is already captured, so why bother. Design says move one line, log it, and prepare the next move before the policy email arrives. You have seen both failure modes in this book. Biofuel mandates that locked acreage. Platform metrics mistaken for bank balances. Panic that flattened assistive pipelines disabled people already depend on. Steelmanning was never softness. It was how you keep energy aimed at the blueprint instead of the hammer. The work that began in loss—attention sharpened when something ended—does not need to end in opinion. It can end in habit. Observe before you intervene. Catch and store what your household and your enterprise cannot afford to waste again: attention, kilowatt-hours, calendar, trust. Read edges: where your lease ends, where your license terminates, where your watershed starts. Refuse dead ends only a vendor can reboot. That discipline is the same whether you are debugging a pipeline or reading a permit. The future is not saved by nostalgia for a world before tools. It is not saved by refusal so broad that incumbents keep the warehouse and the data. It is earned by people who propose better systems than the broken ones—and who live inside the answers long enough to know which lines moved. You used the window to buy calendar back. Spend what remains on arrangements that still make sense when the terms change. Build the ramp. Walk it. Teach the next person where the footing is solid. The ascent was never upward on someone else's chart. It was outward—toward ground you can tend, work you can defend, and tools that know their place in the stack. Appendices A through C turn that stack into checklists you can run at a kitchen table: a tool filter, thirty skeptical use cases, a twelve-month plan keyed to cash months. They add no new theory. They give the work a calendar. Welcome to the work. No new empirical claims in this chapter; exemplars callback prior chapters. Appendices A–C: see each appendix citation lock. Re-verify primary sources at publication when adjacent chapters are locked. Not financial, legal, tax, agronomic, or engineering advice.

parts.title: Appendix A — The Window of Ascent Tool Filter
parts.excerpt: This appendix is not a purity test. It is a decision stack you run before a tool earns a recurring place in your week—whether that tool is a grazing app…
parts.text: Appendix A — The Window of Ascent Tool Filter This appendix is not a purity test. It is a decision stack you run before a tool earns a recurring place in your week—whether that tool is a grazing app, a hosted model, a password manager, or a diesel pump you are about to finance. The filter folds the book's recurring questions—what you are building, who benefits when a product drifts, who owns the interrupt—into one pass you can run in ten minutes at a kitchen table or in a terminal window. How to use it: pick one tool under consideration. Answer each section honestly. A string of "no" answers is not a moral victory—it is a signal to redesign the task, choose a different vendor tier, or keep the offline path you already have. 1. Target alignment - Can you state—in one sentence—which arrangement this tool serves: autonomy, land access, resilience, paid work, or access to public life? - If the tool disappeared tomorrow, would you lose a skill you still need on a bad Tuesday, or only a convenience you can replace? - Does this tool move a number you track (see Appendix C), or only a feeling? - Would you still choose this tool if you could not post about choosing it? 2. Scale and maintenance (Schumacher-style) E.F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful argument is often reduced to "small good, big bad." The useful slice is sharper: right-sized for the load, maintainable by the people who depend on it, repairable without a global supply chain miracle. - Is the tool sized for your operation—not a demo farm, not a Fortune 500 procurement deck? - Can you explain how it works to a neighbor—or to your future self at 11 p.m.—without reading marketing copy? - Who maintains it when it breaks: you, a local tech, a vendor ticket queue, or nobody? - If maintenance requires a subscription, is the subscription price stable relative to your cash months (Appendix C metric)? - For physical tools: can parts be sourced regionally? For software: can you export your data in a format you can read? 3. Ownership and exit - Do you own the object, the data, and the workflow—or rent all three? - What happens at lease renewal, terms-of-service update, or price doubling? Have you read the clause that governs that moment? - Is there an offline or self-hosted path for work that must survive a vendor email? - If export exists, have you tested it once—not "planned to test"? - For land-linked tools: does the lease allow the improvement you are about to finance? 4. Incentive trace - What metric likely governs this product's roadmap: engagement, seat count, upsell, data harvest, or task completion? - Did the tool arrive with a legitimate purpose—access, communication, productivity—and drift toward spectacle? If yes, is the original use case still supported on your tier? - For assistive or adaptive tools: if the vendor pivots, do you have a fallback that preserves participation—not only convenience? 5. Attention and security - Who can interrupt you through this tool—and can you silence it without a fight? - Does the default UI train return visits or task completion? - Are credentials for this tool behind a password manager and multi-factor authentication on the account that resets them? - For hosted AI: does your input leave the machine? If yes, is that acceptable for the sensitivity of the data? 6. AI-specific pass (NIST AI RMF, plain language) The National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes an AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF; verify current title and URL at https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework before print) organized around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. You do not need the PDF on your lap to borrow the structure. Govern - Who in your household or enterprise approves new AI uses—and who owns the mistake? - Is there a list of tasks where AI is off limits (high harm, licensed profession, safety sign-off)? Map - What is the input (PDF, email, sensor log, code repo)? - What is the output (draft, label, summary, code patch)? - Who is downstream if the output is wrong? Measure - Have you logged one week on one task: minutes before, minutes after, errors caught, errors that would have shipped? - If the log shows no gain, have you adjusted the design instead of buying a more expensive model? Manage - Where is the human verification step—and is it proportional to harm? - Where is the archive of what shipped (email sent, code merged, rate applied to field)? 7. The ten-minute scorecard Copy this block once per tool decision: | Question | Yes / No / N/A | Notes | |----------|----------------|-------| | Serves your stated build target | | | | Right-sized; maintainable by you or local help | | | | Data export tested | | | | Offline or fallback path exists | | | | Incentive drift checked on your tier | | | | Interrupt ownership acceptable | | | | Verification step defined | | | | Harm if wrong: low / medium / high | | | High harm + weak verification = stop. Medium harm + strong verification = proceed with logging. Low harm + weak verification = acceptable for drafts; still archive. 8. What this filter refuses to do - It does not tell you to avoid all hosted tools. It tells you to know what you rented. - It does not replace professional advice for law, tax, medicine, engineering, or food safety. - It does not guarantee purity. It guarantees you looked at the blueprint before blaming the hammer. Run the filter when you add a tool. Run it again when the vendor sends a pricing email. The window stays open only while you still know what you are building. Normative appendix; no external statistics. NIST AI RMF: verify publication title, version, and URL at citation pass (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Schumacher references are conceptual, not bibliographic requirements. Not financial, legal, tax, agronomic, or engineering advice.

parts.text: Appendix B — Thirty Practical AI Use Cases for Skeptics The main text named six buckets—learn, plan, draft, code, admin, research—and refused to sell a prompt list as a book. This appendix expands the buckets into thirty workflows you can inspect, adapt, or reject. Each entry follows the same skeleton: - Inputs — what you feed the system - Model class — hosted chat, local open-weight, or speech/vision assistive stack (pick what matches your privacy and cost bar) - Verification — the step that separates leverage from lottery - Harm if wrong — low / medium / high (high always means licensed human review, not "try again") Ordinary includes disabled people running load-bearing access pipelines. Several entries below are written for that reality—not as inspiration, but as design. No entry below replaces a clinician, lawyer, accountant, engineer, or food-safety sign-off. Learn (1–5) These five workflows help you read primary material faster without treating the model as the primary. 1. Extension bulletin glossary - Inputs: PDF soil bulletin; list of terms you do not know - Model class: hosted or local text model - Verification: open the PDF; check every definition against the primary text - Harm if wrong: medium (bad agronomy decisions downstream) 2. Equipment manual triage - Inputs: scanner PDF of a used tractor manual; your symptom list - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: locate the cited page in the manual; confirm part numbers before ordering - Harm if wrong: medium 3. Codebase orientation for a volunteer - Inputs: repo README + one module; newcomer questions - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: senior maintainer reads answers; newcomer follows links and flags hallucinated paths - Harm if wrong: low for reading; medium if they commit code on faith 4. Second-language study prompts - Inputs: chapter text you are assigned; target language - Model class: hosted - Verification: instructor or native speaker checks generated exercises - Harm if wrong: low 5. Safety training quiz draft - Inputs: your shop's actual procedures (written); job role - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: foreperson or safety lead rewrites anything that contradicts posted rules - Harm if wrong: high—treat model output as draft only Plan (6–10) Planning entries fail when they ignore lease clauses, frost dates, and permits the model cannot see from a prompt alone. 6. Three-field rotation sketch - Inputs: lease constraints, equipment passes, frost dates, cover-crop goal - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: extension agent or experienced neighbor; soil test; lease clause check - Harm if wrong: medium 7. Market garden weekly task board - Inputs: crop list, stand hours, volunteer count - Model class: hosted - Verification: walk the field; delete tasks that ignore mud, frost, or equipment overlap - Harm if wrong: low 8. Small retrofit scope options - Inputs: photos + dimensions of a root cellar or cooler wall; budget band - Model class: hosted - Verification: licensed contractor or experienced builder before spending money - Harm if wrong: high for structural work—model proposes questions, not approvals 9. Event run-of-show draft - Inputs: prior year schedule; vendor constraints; accessibility needs (captioning, seating, quiet room) - Model class: hosted - Verification: human checks times, permits, ADA routes, and vendor contracts - Harm if wrong: medium 10. Personal budget scenario labels - Inputs: anonymized expense categories; goal from Appendix C (cash months) - Model class: hosted or local on your machine only - Verification: you reconcile against bank exports; model never sees credentials - Harm if wrong: medium—still not tax advice Draft (11–15) Drafting is where verification is most often skipped because the output looks finished. 11. Co-op pickup time change email - Inputs: two prior member emails for tone; new date/time; fee rules - Model class: hosted - Verification: coordinator reads for wrong dates, wrong fees, accidental promises - Harm if wrong: low–medium (forty families at the wrong dock) 12. Grant narrative first pass - Inputs: funder rubric; bullet list of your project facts - Model class: hosted - Verification: grant writer or board member; every statistic traced to a primary source - Harm if wrong: medium (reputation + deadline) 13. Zoning comment letter draft - Inputs: your stake; ordinance section headings; hearing date - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: read the statute sections yourself; lawyer if property rights are at stake - Harm if wrong: high for legal outcomes—drafting aid only 14. Job posting plain language - Inputs: role tasks; wage band; physical requirements stated honestly - Model class: hosted - Verification: HR or owner checks for discriminatory phrasing and wrong wage statements - Harm if wrong: medium–high 15. Meeting notes to action items - Inputs: audio transcript or rough notes - Model class: hosted or speech-to-text + text model - Verification: chair approves action list; assignees confirm they accept the task - Harm if wrong: low–medium Code (16–20) Codegen saves keystrokes; it does not save review when money or safety moves through the diff. 16. CSV ledger parser - Inputs: sample export from co-op software; expected columns - Model class: hosted codegen - Verification: unit tests; empty file + duplicate row edge cases; human reads diff - Harm if wrong: medium (wrong payouts) 17. API client scaffold - Inputs: OpenAPI snippet; auth method - Model class: hosted codegen - Verification: replay one request in curl with headers you typed - Harm if wrong: medium 18. Rename columns for portal upload - Inputs: spreadsheet headers; portal template - Model class: local script assist - Verification: portal accepts file; spot-check five rows - Harm if wrong: low–medium 19. Terraform/module stub for homelab - Inputs: desired services; network diagram in prose - Model class: hosted or local - Verification: plan before apply; senior reviewer if production - Harm if wrong: high if exposed to internet—lab only without review 20. Test fixtures from examples - Inputs: three real anonymized records - Model class: hosted codegen - Verification: tests fail on intentionally broken input you add - Harm if wrong: medium Admin (21–25) Admin tasks look low-stakes until a missed renewal date or a wrong fee line hits. 21. Invoice pile sorted by due date - Inputs: scanned envelopes or PDF folder - Model class: hosted vision or text - Verification: cross-check every date against the PDF in the pile - Harm if wrong: medium (late fees) 22. License renewal calendar - Inputs: list of business, vehicle, and pesticide/applicator licenses - Model class: hosted - Verification: pull each renewal from the issuing agency website - Harm if wrong: medium–high 23. Travel reimbursement line items - Inputs: receipt photos; employer policy excerpt - Model class: hosted - Verification: finance clerk; policy PDF open beside the draft - Harm if wrong: medium 24. Inbound email routing labels - Inputs: sample inbox export (redacted) - Model class: hosted - Verification: you review a week of false positives/negatives before automating - Harm if wrong: low–medium 25. Plain-language summary of a vendor contract - Inputs: contract PDF - Model class: hosted only if confidentiality allows - Verification: read termination, auto-renew, liability, and data clauses in the original; lawyer for high stakes - Harm if wrong: high Research (26–30) Research entries carry the highest integrity bar: open the source or do not cite it. 26. Statute section map - Inputs: bill number or municipal code URL; your question in one sentence - Model class: hosted with citation links - Verification: click every cited section; headings must match - Harm if wrong: high for compliance decisions 27. Supplier comparison table - Inputs: spec sheets you provide; weighted criteria you define - Model class: hosted - Verification: call one supplier; confirm lead time and price on the p

parts.title: Appendix C — Twelve-Month Ascent Plan

parts.text: Appendix C — Twelve-Month Ascent Plan This appendix is a calendar skeleton, not a life script. It assumes you have named what you are building—land, autonomy, resilience, paid work, or access—and that you are willing to measure progress in numbers that survive a bad Tuesday. Primary metric: cash months Pick one headline number for the year: Months of fixed expenses covered in cash — household and enterprise separated if both exist. Fixed means rent or mortgage, insurance, utilities, loan minimums, subscriptions you cannot cancel in thirty days, and payroll you owe if you employ anyone. Variable means feed, seed, materials, cloud bills that scale with use, and market spending. Why this metric: it crosses place-first and systems-first lives. A grazier and a contract developer both know what happens when that number hits zero. It connects to the four-number alignment exercise and does not require you to win a productivity lottery to see progress. Secondary metrics (optional, logged quarterly): soil organic matter or cover-crop success on rented ground; one dependency you reduced; one pipeline archived with verification notes. Before Month 1 — one afternoon setup 1. Write your build sentence on paper: "I am trying to build because ." 2. List fixed expenses monthly total (two columns if household + enterprise). 3. Count cash and cash-equivalents you could reach in seven days without selling illiquid assets. 4. Divide (3) by (2). That is your starting cash months. Round down. 5. Open a single running log—paper, spreadsheet, or plain text— titled Ascent Log. One line per week is enough. Month 1 — Name and measure (January, northern temperate) Cash: refresh starting cash months; note lowest week of the month. Land / place (if applicable): inventory seeds, tools, and storage; repair what failed last season before ordering new. Systems: list every recurring subscription and its renewal date; run Appendix A on the three largest lines. Policy clock (verify dates at publication): note tax-document season approaching; check USDA NASS land-value summary update if land entry is in your target. Log prompt: What dependency would hurt most if it vanished in thirty days? Month 2 — Lease and license read (February) Cash: move one week's fixed expenses into a separate buffer account if banking allows; if not, mark an envelope. Land: order soil tests if frost allows sampling in your region; read lease renewal window. Systems: export data from one hosted tool you rely on; store offline. Access: if you use assistive AI, read the vendor's current privacy policy and termination clause. Log prompt: Did export work? What format? Month 3 — First quarter close (March) Cash: recompute cash months; compare to Month 1. Land: finalize crop plan or grazing chart for the season; confirm equipment maintenance schedule. Systems: pick one Appendix B use case; run one week with minutes logged. Four-number check: cash months; land/facility target band; income mix percentages; one dependency + first reduction step. Log prompt: Which number embarrassed you? Stay there. Month 4 — Plant and pipeline (April) Cash: trim one subscription that failed Appendix A; redirect half the savings to buffer. Land: planting window tasks per your zone; record actual dates, not plan dates. Systems: archive one completed model-assisted workflow (email sent, code merged, rate applied). Log prompt: What shipped with verification? Month 5 — Attention audit (May) Cash: no new recurring spend without deleting or downgrading something else. Land: scout fields or gardens weekly; note pest or drought stress early. Systems: run an interrupt audit—who can ping you, and can you silence it? Log prompt: One hour reclaimed—where did it go? Month 6 — Midyear review (June) Cash: recompute cash months; target +0.25 months improvement over March unless a known large expense explains the flat line. Land: midseason yield or forage estimate; adjust market or stocking plan. Systems: rotate passwords on email and domain registrar; confirm MFA. Policy clock (verify dates at publication): watch for mid-year software price changes; if you ship models or weights across borders, read EU AI Act GPAI obligations and U.S. BIS export-control notices from primary sources—do not react to headlines alone. Log prompt: Is your build sentence still true? Month 7 — Heat and load (July) Cash: model one bad month (sales −20% or hay purchase spike); does buffer survive? Land: irrigation, shade, or livestock heat protocols; log water use if metered. Systems: if using local inference, log power draw one week—kWh matters on marginal grids. Log prompt: What broke in the bad-month model? Month 8 — Community credit (August) Cash: pay vendors on time; note any stretched terms you accepted. Land: preservation, drying, or early cover-crop seeding per your rotation. Systems: backup restore drill—actually restore one file from backup. Log prompt: Who would vouch for you locally if you needed a favor? Month 9 — Third quarter close (September) Cash: recompute cash months; compare to March and June. Land: harvest or grazing records on paper before photos; weights and dates for your memory, not the platform's. Systems: second Appendix B use case trial OR deepen the first pipeline with eval notes. Four-number check: repeat the alignment exercise (cash months, land/facility band, income mix, one dependency). Log prompt: Income mix—did percentages sum to reality? Month 10 — Winter prep (October) Cash: set aside known large annual bills (insurance, property tax installment if applicable—verify your jurisdiction). Land: put equipment under cover; order only what maintenance logs prove you need. Systems: run Appendix A on any new tool adopted since spring. Policy clock: USDA NASS land-value summaries often publish in autumn—update your land/facility target band from primary NASS tables (Land Values summary; verify release month for the current survey year), not headlines. Log prompt: What did you almost buy to avoid a hard decision? Month 11 — Reduce dependency (November) Cash: identify one platform, landlord, employer, or single-client dependency; take the first reduction step (second vendor quote, second client conversation, lease negotiation question). Land: soil test results into rotation notes; plan amendments you can defend to the landowner. Systems: document one offline path that worked. Log prompt: What would you do if the vendor email arrived tomorrow? Month 12 — Year close and next ramp (December) Cash: final cash months for the year; note delta from Month 1 in the Ascent Log cover page. Land: equipment winterization; seed inventory; review what varieties earned their row space. Systems: delete accounts you no longer use; export once more from tools you keep. Review: re-read the conclusion's builder exemplars—grazier protocol, food hub calendar check—and mark which pattern you lived this year. Next year: raise cash-month target by 0.25–0.5 if structurally possible; if not, name the structural blocker honestly (lease, health, debt service) and pick one transitional move instead of punishing yourself with a fantasy number. Seasonal note for other climates Northern-hemisphere temperate months above map roughly to: | Month | Southern temperate shift | Frost-free tropics emphasis | |-------|--------------------------|-----------------------------| | Jan–Mar | Jul–Sep | Wet/dry season planning | | Apr–Jun | Oct–Dec | Planting/rain alignment | | Jul–Sep | Jan–Mar | Heat/water stress | | Oct–Dec | Apr–Jun | Harvest/store or cyclone prep | Shift land tasks; keep cash months and four-number checks on the same calendar so place-first and systems-first readers share one spine. What this plan refuses to promise - It does not prescribe dollar amounts. Your county's rent and your enterprise's payroll are yours to model. - It does not replace accountants, lawyers, agronomists, or therapists. - It does not treat AI as a step. parts.text: Colophon Assisted drafting This manuscript was written in collaboration with AI tools used as drafting and revision assistants—not as authors of record. AI role: prose generation and multi-pass revision against voicecalibration.md, revisionworkflow.md, and chapter research companions in srcmaterial/research/. Reader takeaway: If this book argues that tools inherit incentives, its own production is a case study.
